searches.note: Twenty three searches of a share of twenty eight, five left unspent, none of them the author's. One was shared across the group: the Paraje Altamira geographical indication, read through the decree's text on WIPO Lex. Four were restricted to a house's own domain (Catena twice, Zuccardi's sheets, Norton's Privada page); the others kept the house's domain, and where the author had leant on them Wikipedia, Winebow and Lay and Wheeler, out, so that each second source would be independent. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail stood in one page alone that is not the house speaking of itself, it was cut or said with less; the house's own claims stay told as its account.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Wine Anorak, a wine blog or two, a critic's subscription site) are cited neither in the fragment nor here; a critic's site whose address names a living writer is described, never cited by address.

The serving temperatures follow the Codex's service reference: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius for the full reds, 15 to 17 for Finca Piedra Infinita as a medium red poured a little cool; no air is promised to soften tannin.
The edits were made in place by exact string replacement, keeping the author's layout, and linted sound with five records refuted.

tested: The founding: Nicola Catena's arrival in 1898 and first Malbec vineyard of 1902 (Wikipedia, the Catena Institute, Montecristo; one merchant's 1920 is an outlier). Sound.

The son's belief that Malbec could stand beside the wines of France: the house's brochure and a label note, both its own account, as the record hedges it; one trade feature has the son seeing Malbec as a blending component, so the hedge is kept. Sound.
The grandson's Berkeley years: 1981 in one of the house's own pages, the beginning of 1982 in an interview it publishes, 1982 to 1985 in its Adrianna brochure. Changed to the early 1980s.
The Adrianna Vineyard: planted in 1992 and named for the grandson's youngest daughter (the house's Adrianna page and brochure); another of its pages says the mid 1990s. 1992 stands, open.
The vineyard at about 1,450 metres and the River Stones parcel at about 1,366 (Wine Folly's guide, the house's sheets; one listing 4,757 feet for the vineyard). Sound.
The Malbec from Lot 18 of the Angélica vineyard: the house and a critic's site; the vineyard's date of around 1930 is the house's, but the same critic's site finds it in a census of 1924. Changed.

The parcel's white stones coated in calcium carbonate, an ancient riverbed: the house's 2018 sheet through Winebow's files, Wine Folly. Sound. The shortened label name River from about 2019: Vinissimus, Trialto, Shop Wine Direct. Sound.

The making: whole bunches in part in one vintage, foudres of 500 litres and concrete for up to sixteen months in 2021, a 2,000 litre foudre and the rest in steel by a critic's note of 2021 quoted by a merchant, eighteen to twenty one months on other sheets. Changed to well over a year, the vessels changing.
The label: no sheet read shows an appellation field; the Mendoza line now claims less. The respelling of Gualtallary was in no source. Both changed.

Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach; 1853 for Malbec's arrival agrees with the Codex's own records. Rules: no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. The blend Nicolás Catena Zapata is named as a label only; see open.

changed.was: Cold soaked for some days, then fermented over two to three weeks, with part of the vat in whole bunches in some later vintages. The wine rests eighteen months to two years in French oak: barrels in the early vintages, large foudres of some 2,200 litres and more than ten years old in later ones.
changed.now: Cold soaked for some days, then fermented over two to three weeks, with part of the vat in whole bunches in some later vintages. The wine then rests for well over a year in French oak, in barrels in the early vintages and in large, old foudres in later ones; the months and the vessels change with the vintage.
changed.why: The months and vessels differ by vintage: up to sixteen months in 500 litre foudres and concrete in 2021, a 2,000 litre foudre and steel in a critic's note of that year, eighteen to twenty one months on other sheets; the record now says well over a year and that the vessels change.

tested: The founding of 1998 by Argentine and Italian friends: the Drinks Business (the project began in 1998) and the library, with two accounts naming Argentine and Italian founders; one guide dates the brand to 1995. Sound.
Finca Altamira 1999 as the house's first wine, released in 2000: the Drinks Business and Cellar Tours. Sound.
The SPI group of 2011: a majority by Wine Spectator and Just Drinks, a major stake by Decanter; the record's bought into holds either way. Sound.

The making: cement vats, pump overs, no cold soak, no enzymes, no acid correction (a merchant's listing beside the house's sheet); new French oak for fourteen or fifteen months in older vintages (a critic's note, Wine.com 2007) and thirteen months mostly new in 2019 (the house); bottled unfined and unfiltered (Robb Report). Sound.

The sites: La Consulta, about 1,050 to 1,100 metres (Wine Folly, a merchant, the house); Finca Mirador in Medrano and Finca Bella Vista in Perdriel, Luján de Cuyo (Wine Folly's guide, a merchant). Sound.
The place: the winery stands on Calle Cobos at Perdriel in Luján de Cuyo (Afar, En Primeur Club, Pearl), not in La Consulta. Changed.
Paraje Altamira recognised as a geographical indication by the INV in 2013 (Resolution 44/2013, on WIPO Lex), widened in 2017. Sound.

Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach. Rules: nobody living named (the founders and the founding oenologist are not named), no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: The founding of 1963 by an engineer who planted a vineyard in Maipú to show an irrigation system he had designed, and a winery by 1968 by one of them: several results, among them an importer's profile, Discovery Wine Mendoza and a South American wine guide. Sound.

The first Uco Valley vineyard, Canal Uco in Paraje Altamira, in 2007: a merchant's profile and a critic's site. Sound. The Piedra Infinita vineyard planted in 2009 by one source, undated in the record. Sound.

The winery opened in 2016, built in part with stones of the Piedra Infinita vineyard in its concrete: a critic's site and Discovery Wine Mendoza; one source has a winery completed in 2013. Sound, open on 2013.

The soils: a sandy surface over granite boulders coated in calcium carbonate, on the southern alluvial fan of the Tunuyán river (Wine Adventurer, the importer's Gravascal sheet, a merchant's profile); about 1,100 metres. Changed.

The making: concrete without epoxy and native yeasts (the importer's sheets of 2019 and 2020); used 500 litre French oak barrels beside concrete on the house's sheets of 2014 to 2017, oak barrels and concrete in 2013; concrete alone on the house's sheets of 2019 and 2022, against 30 per cent in 500 litre barrels on the importer's 2019 sheet; no sheet of 2020 or 2021 found. Changed.
Gravascal and Supercal as plots of the vineyard, Concreto as a separate wine: the importer's sheets, a merchant, the house. Sound.

Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach. Rules: the founder and his heirs not named, no price, no score (the winery's places on ranked lists left out), nothing volatile (recent vintages refused by the lint and reworded), British, no dash.

changed.now: Familia Zuccardi's Finca Piedra Infinita is Malbec from a vineyard of granite stones in Paraje Altamira, fermented and aged in concrete rather than new oak. It shows violet, pepper and wet stone over a chalky grip, so pour it a little cool.
changed.why: The house's 2013 sheet names oak barrels without saying used, and later sheets give used barrels then concrete alone; rather than new oak holds for every sheet read and the library's style line, and recent vintages is refused by the lint as volatile.

tested: The first vintage of 1999 (Decanter's review of the 1999, Berry Bros and Rudd, most accounts; one retailer's 2001 an error); founded 1998 by Wine Folly's guide. 1999 stands, open.
The ungrafted Malbec of Las Compuertas, on its own roots since 1929, at about 1,070 metres (a merchant's page, Wine Folly's guide). Sound.

Flood irrigation drowning phylloxera: the house's Savoir-Faire page and Terroir Wines; drip irrigation from stored snowmelt from 2017 by the house. The record says only that the vines were long flooded. Sound.

The grapes: the 1999 60 per cent Cabernet Sauvignon by one listing, the 2021 49 Cabernet to 48 Malbec, the 2022 65 Cabernet to 30, the 2023 57 to 40, Petit Verdot added by vintage. Changed: no grape is said to lead.

The making: small vats of 30 to 80 hectolitres, plot by plot (Millesima, the house's 2021 sheet); picked from 3 to 17 March in 2022, against April on the author's 2021 sheet; thirteen months in 225, 400 and 2,500 litre oak in 2018, sixteen to eighteen months in new and second fill barrels on another account. Changed.

The Altamira vineyard at about 1,150 metres (Millesima). Sound. Terrazas de los Andes founded in 1996 by Moët Hennessy: Wikipedia and one guide page; Château Cheval Blanc's own page calls the Mendoza house a pioneer. Sound, open on a primary.

tested: The founder, Edmund James Palmer Norton (1865 to 1944), an engineer who came to help build the Transandine railway: Geni, Wein-Plus, a Spanish travel account and Wikipedia as the author read it; born on the border of Prussia and Denmark and raised in England by two accounts. Sound.

The founding of 1895 at Perdriel, the first winery south of the Mendoza river, vines brought from France: several results in Spanish and English beside the house; Wine Folly's guide puts the planting in 1985, plainly a slip. Sound.

The purchase of 1989 by the head of the Swarovski crystal house: The Wine Time, Wikipedia, Wein-Plus. Sound. He died in January 2021 (Blick, Il Sussidiario, the Tiroler Tageszeitung), so he is not living; the record still describes him, which is right.

Privada: 40 per cent Malbec and 30 each of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, from the house's oldest vineyards of 50 to 90 years at La Colonia, Lunlunta and Agrelo; a three day cold soak at 8 to 10 degrees and ten days of ferment at 25; appellation Luján de Cuyo (the house's product page and shop); about sixteen months in oak (Vinos de Argentina, a Portuguese merchant). Changed: the appellation, the making.
The first four wineries of the D.O.C. Luján de Cuyo: in no source but the house; the D.O.C. founded in 1989 by a group of producers by one guide. Kept hedged in the story, cut from others.
The name: the house sells it as Privada Family Blend, merchants as Norton Privada or Privada Family Blend; the plan's name stands and the trap now teaches the newer one.

Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach. Rules: the buyer of 1989 and his heirs not named, no price, no score (a medal of 2023 left out), nothing volatile, British, no dash.

picks: All five picks stand. Catena Zapata, Achaval-Ferrer, Familia Zuccardi, Cheval des Andes and Bodega Norton are the houses a sommelier meets first in Mendoza, from the historic first zone and the Uco Valley; no swap of a house is proposed or made.
For the integrator: Blick reports Bodega Norton in court ordered insolvency proceedings; the record tells nothing of the present, and the pick is kept as the historic Luján de Cuyo house of 1895.
